events.note: Alexander Wilson described a breeding place several miles wide running upwards of forty miles through the Kentucky beech woods.
Wilson computed a single flock passing overhead toward the Indiana Territory at 2,230,272,000 birds.
Audubon rode beneath a flight that eclipsed the noon sun; he calculated over 1.1 billion birds in three hours, and the river of pigeons ran for three days.
Audubon's great Kentucky roost: more than three miles wide and forty long, dung inches deep, mature trees snapping under the birds' weight.
The railroad reaches a nesting: some 1.8 million pigeons (150,000 dozen) shipped to city markets in one season, dealers paying 31-56 cents a dozen.
Maj. W. Ross King watched a flight stream past for hours on end — later reckoned at more than 3.7 billion birds.
A column a mile wide and 300 miles long took 14 hours to pass: an estimated 3.5 billion birds, one of the last sky-darkening flights.
Three railcar loads a day for forty days — a reported 11,880,000 birds sent east to market from one small town.
The largest nesting ever recorded: about 850 square miles of central Wisconsin sand country, an estimated 136 million breeding birds.
One of the great mid-1870s Michigan nestings; professional netters shipped birds by the boxcar to Chicago and New York.
The last great nesting: roughly 40 miles long and 3-10 wide near Little Traverse Bay; about 50,000 birds killed a day for nearly five months, over a million shipped by rail and steamer.
A Warren County colony worked over by professional netters — the last recorded visit of the pigeoners to Pennsylvania.
Hundreds of young pigeons clubbed over three days in May; after 1880, nesting in Pennsylvania was only sporadic.
A final sizable Michigan nesting in the years after Petoskey — found by the netters and raided like all the rest.
The last nestings of large size anywhere took place in central Wisconsin this year; none of comparable scale ever formed again.
The last known mass nesting attempt, northeast of Wautoma, was broken up by indiscriminate shooting; by June the birds had abandoned it.
Ontario's last confirmed specimen, shot in September 1891.
The last rookery confirmed in Ontario: about 20 birds and 12 nests — a species of billions reduced to a dozen nests.
Wisconsin's last fully authenticated wild passenger pigeon, shot in September 1899.
March 24, 1900: 14-year-old Press Clay Southworth shot a female — mounted as 'Buttons' — the last fully confirmed wild passenger pigeon.
A bird reportedly shot on April 3, 1902 — among the last credible reports of a wild passenger pigeon.
September 1, 1914, about 1 p.m.: Martha, the last passenger pigeon on Earth, died in her cage at roughly 29 years old.

timeline.event: An estimated 3 to 5 billion passenger pigeons — perhaps one of every four birds in North America — range the eastern forests.
Audubon's Ohio River flight darkens the sky for three days; he calculates over 1.1 billion birds passing in three hours.
Railroads reach the nestings: about 1.8 million pigeons shipped to market from a single colony near Plattsburgh, New York.
An Ohio Senate committee rejects protection, declaring the pigeon so 'wonderfully prolific' that no ordinary destruction can lessen it.
Telegraph and rail industrialize the hunt: professional pigeoners, hundreds strong, now track and reach every large nesting within days.
The largest nesting ever recorded covers ~850 square miles of central Wisconsin — an estimated 136 million breeding birds.
Petoskey, Michigan: the last great nesting. Roughly 50,000 birds killed per day for nearly five months; over a million shipped.
The last large nestings form in central Wisconsin; every later attempt is broken up before the young can fledge.
The final known mass nesting attempt, near Wautoma, Wisconsin, is abandoned under gunfire.
March 24: a farm boy in Pike County, Ohio shoots the last fully confirmed wild passenger pigeon.
The American Ornithologists' Union offers a $1,500 reward for an undisturbed nesting pair. It is never claimed.
September 1: Martha, the last of her species, dies at the Cincinnati Zoo. The population is zero.

facts: Discovered in March 1878 in the hardwoods near Crooked Lake and Little Traverse Bay: a nesting about 40 miles long and 3 to 10 miles wide — roughly 100,000 acres of nests, with some 150,000 acres inside its limits.
Word traveled by telegraph, and within days hundreds of professional pigeoners — estimates run from 600 netters to 2,000 or more people working the colony — had converged from across the country.
At the peak, roughly 50,000 birds were killed each day, and the pace held for nearly five months; dead birds alone left by rail at an estimated 12,500 per day.
Iced barrels went south on the Grand Rapids & Indiana Railroad and by steamer from the Petoskey docks; live birds were crated out for trap-shooting clubs.
More than a million birds were shipped in all; counting squabs left to starve, spoilage, and waste, the true kill was far higher.

H.B. Roney's small enforcement party documented the slaughter and pressed charges under Michigan's weak nesting law — token fines changed nothing, but his 1879 expose became the hunt's most damning record.

It was the species' last great nesting anywhere. Survivors that tried to re-nest that summer were followed and broken up, the immense colonies the pigeon's biology required never assembled again, and extinction followed within 36 years.

facts: Flocks cruised at up to about 60 miles per hour and foraged scores of miles from a roost in a day — a nomadic species that followed the beech and oak mast crops across the eastern forest.

Each pair laid a single egg per nesting. Survival depended on colonies so vast they simply swamped every predator — a strategy that collapsed once the colonies were broken, so hunters never needed to kill the last bird, only the last great nesting.
At the big roosts, mature trees two feet thick snapped under the weight of perched birds, dung lay inches deep, and the understory died — observers compared the aftermath to the track of a tornado.

After the Civil War, telegraph and rail industrialized the hunt: several hundred to over a thousand full-time professional pigeoners followed the flocks year-round and could converge on any reported nesting within days.

Pigeons were the cheapest meat in eastern cities, often selling for around 50 cents a dozen; squabs were a restaurant delicacy, and live-trapped birds fed the trap-shooting circuit by the tens of thousands.
The clearing of the eastern beech and oak forests shrank the pigeon's food supply and nesting grounds at the very moment the market hunt peaked.
From 1909 to 1912 the American Ornithologists' Union offered a $1,500 reward for a single undisturbed nesting pair. No one ever claimed it.

Martha — named for Martha Washington — hatched in captivity and never flew wild. After her death on September 1, 1914, she was frozen in a 300-pound block of ice and shipped to the Smithsonian, where her mounted body remains.

The pigeon's disappearance stunned a public that had thought it inexhaustible, and helped drive America's first wildlife protection laws, from the Lacey Act of 1900 to the Migratory Bird Treaty Act of 1918.
